title: is vs == : Identity vs Equality

glossary.definition: The unique memory address or location of an object in a computer, confirming it is the exact same object. Example: `id(a) == id(b)` is the underlying check that `a is b` performs.

Objects or classes that are designed so that only one unique instance of them can ever exist in a program. Example: `None`, `True`, and `False` are singletons in Python — `x is None` is always the right check.

overview.what:
The `==` operator compares the VALUES of two objects (equality), while the `is` operator compares the MEMORY ADDRESSES of two objects (identity). Two distinct objects can have the exact same value (`==` is `True`), but because they live in different places in memory, they are not the same object (`is` is `False`). Think of `==` as asking 'Do these two houses look identical?' and `is` as asking 'Are these two addresses pointing to the exact same house?'.

In Python, `is` checks if `id(a) == id(b)`. Mixing up `is` and `==` causes subtle bugs when comparing collections. Use `==` when you want to know if the data matches, and use `is` when you need to know if two variables refer to the exact same object in memory.

  a = [1, 2]
  b = [1, 2]
  print(a == b)  # True
  print(a is b)  # False (trap!)

Comparing mutable structures with `is` fails unexpectedly because Python creates a new object in memory for each list. This behavior is covered fully in `mutable-vs-immutable`.

Another sharp edge is integer and string interning. Python caches small integers and short strings for performance, making `is` sometimes appear to work for value comparison.

  a = 256
  b = 256
  print(a is b)  # True (interned)
  
  x = 1000
  y = 1000
  print(x is y)  # False (not interned!)

Never use `is` to compare numbers or strings, even if it happens to work for small values. The only time you should consistently use `is` is when checking for singletons like `None`, `True`, or `False`.
overview.why: Mixing up `is` and `==` causes subtle bugs. Use `==` when you want to know if the data matches. Only use `is` when you need to know if two variables refer to the exact same object in memory (most commonly, checking `x is None`).

why_learning_this: Preventing subtle bugs when comparing collections

common_mistakes.title: Using `is` for value comparison
common_mistakes.explanation: Using `is` instead of `==` for strings or numbers might sometimes work due to Python caching (interning) small integers and short strings, but it will randomly fail for larger values or dynamic inputs. Always use `==` for value comparison.

common_mistakes.title: Using `==` to check for None
common_mistakes.explanation: While `x == None` works, the Pythonic and safer way is `x is None`. Some objects (like `pandas` `DataFrame`s or `SQLAlchemy` models) override `__eq__` (which powers `==`) to return an array of booleans or a query expression, which breaks the truth value testing. The `is None` check cannot be overridden.

recall_questions.q: What is the difference between `==` and `is`?
recall_questions.answer: `==` checks if the values are equal (equality), while `is` checks if they are the exact same object in memory (identity).

recall_questions.q: When is it appropriate to use the `is` operator?
recall_questions.answer: When you need to check if two variables point to the exact same object, most commonly when checking for singletons like `None`.

recall_questions.q: Why is it dangerous to use `is` to compare integers or strings for equality?
recall_questions.answer: Because Python caches (interns) small integers and short strings, `is` might sometimes return `True` for identical values, but it will unexpectedly return `False` for larger or dynamically generated numbers and strings.

understanding_checks.question: What will the following code output?
understanding_checks.code:
a = [1, 2]
b = [1, 2]
print(a == b)
print(a is b)
understanding_checks.why: `a` and `b` have the same values, so `a == b` is `True`. However, they are two distinct list objects in memory, so `a is b` evaluates to `False`.

understanding_checks.question: Why is it recommended to use `x is None` instead of `x == None`?
understanding_checks.answer: Because `is` guarantees an identity check, preventing bugs if an object overrides `==` to behave unexpectedly.
understanding_checks.why: Using `== None` triggers the `__eq__` method, which some libraries override to return custom objects instead of a simple boolean. `is None` directly compares memory addresses and cannot be overridden.

understanding_checks.question: What will the following code output?
understanding_checks.code:
x = 1000
y = 1000
print(x is y)
print(x == y)
understanding_checks.why: Since `1000` is a large integer, Python does not intern it by default, so `x` and `y` point to different memory addresses (`x is y` is `False`). However, their values are identical, so `x == y` is `True`.

practice_tasks.title: Fix the singleton comparison
practice_tasks.prompt: The `process_data` function currently uses `==` to check if the result is `None`. This works most of the time but can be unsafe. Modify the function to use the correct operator for checking identity against singletons like `None`.

code_walkthrough.code:
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = [1, 2, 3]
print(a == b)
print(a is b)

aha_moment.prediction: What will these two prints output?
aha_moment.why: Even though `a` and `b` have identical contents (so `a == b` is `True`), lists are mutable objects. Python creates a brand new list in memory every time `[1, 2, 3]` is evaluated. Therefore `x` and `y` point to different memory addresses, and `x is y` is `False`.

challenge.title: Safe None Checking
challenge.prompt: You are writing a database connector. Write a function `process_record(record)` that takes a `record` (which could be a dictionary or `None`). If `record` is exactly `None`, return the string `'No data'`. Otherwise, return the string `'Processing'`. You must use the safest comparison operator for `None`.
